Series::isreal¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::isreal() const

What It Answers¶

isreal() classifies every element independently and returns a Boolean Series with exactly the receiver’s shape. A non-complex element is always real. A complex element is real precisely when its imaginary component compares equal to zero; the real component may have any finite or infinite value.

This is a value predicate, not a dtype query. Use is_complex() when the question is whether the storage dtype can represent imaginary components. Use isreal() when a complex-valued computation has already happened and the question is which resulting lanes actually lie on the real axis.

The distinction matters because one complex Series can contain both kinds of lanes. A value such as 2 - 0i is real, including when the imaginary zero is negative. A value with an imaginary NaN is not real because NaN does not equal zero.

Result Contract¶

  • The result has dtype bool, the same rank and extents as the receiver, and lives on the same platform.

  • Real, integer, and Boolean receivers produce true in every lane.

  • Complex receivers compare only the imaginary component with zero. The real component does not affect classification.

  • The operation allocates a new Boolean result and does not mutate the receiver.

  • The predicate is discrete and does not create a reverse-mode derivative. Apply it as a mask; do not expect sensitivity to pass through the decision.

  • Empty inputs produce empty Boolean results with the same shape.

Examples¶

1. A real-valued matrix is real in every lane¶

const auto values = pluss::make_series({{1.0, -2.0}, {0.0, 4.0}});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, values.isreal());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ true true ⎤
⎣ true true ⎦

The method does not ask whether the values are positive, finite, or nonzero. All native real-valued lanes satisfy the predicate.

2. A complex matrix is classified lane by lane¶

using Complex = std::complex<double>;

const auto values = pluss::make_series(
    std::vector<Complex>{{1.0, 0.0}, {2.0, -0.0},
                         {3.0, 4.0}, {0.0, -2.0}},
    {2, 2});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, values.isreal());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡  true  true ⎤
⎣ false false ⎦

Both positive and negative zero imaginary components compare equal to zero. The final two values have nonzero imaginary components and therefore produce false.

3. Scalar rank is preserved¶

const auto scalar = pluss::make_series(4.5);
pluss::series::print(std::cout, scalar.isreal());

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=true

The result is still rank zero. isreal() never adds, removes, or flattens an axis.

Performance¶

The operation is linear in numel(). Non-complex inputs use an all-true fast path; complex inputs inspect one imaginary component per lane. The result is a new contiguous Boolean allocation, so retain it when the same mask will be reused by several later operations.

See Also¶

  • real() extracts real components as numeric values.

  • imag() extracts the component tested by this predicate.

  • is_complex() queries storage capability rather than lane values.

  • isfinite() classifies finite numeric values.
